card: Paper card. Question: How can massive amounts of interstitial elements (O, C, N) be dissolved in a metallic host lattice without forming brittle ceramic phases, while simultaneously achieving near-theoretical strength and large deformability?. System: TiNbZr-O-C-N massive interstitial solid solution (MISS) alloys, specifically (TiNbZr)86O12C1N1 (at%) referred to as O-12 MISS alloy, and reference alloys (TiNbZr)92O6C1N1 (O-6), (TiNbZr)92O8 (O-8), and equiatomic TiNbZr. Processing: Magnetron sputtering on Si (001) substrates with Ar pressure of 0.3 Pa and substrate bias power of 90 W, followed by annealing in a vacuum (10−2 Pa) at 500 °C for 2 h to promote interstitial diffusion. Test conditions: Uniaxial compression of micropillars (diameter 1.0–1.6 μm) at ambient temperature with a nominal strain rate of 5 × 10−3 s−1; in-situ SEM bending and tensile tests at ambient temperature. Findings: The O-12 MISS alloy contains 12 at% interstitial O with no oxides, carbides, or nitrides formed.; The alloy exhibits an ultrahigh compressive yield strength of 4.2 ± 0.2 GPa.; The alloy maintains large deformability of 65% strain at ambient temperature without localized shear deformation.; The shear stress ratio τy/G reaches 1/18, approaching the theoretical limit of ~1/10.; In bending tests, the O-12 alloy shows an ultrahigh flow stress of 5.6 ± 0.5 GPa and withstands a tensile strain of 54%.; Grain refinement occurs during deformation, reducing grain diameters from 20–50 nm to 5–20 nm at ~65% strain.; C and N segregate to grain boundaries with concentrations of 1.8 ± 0.3 at% and 1.0 ± 0.2 at%, respectively.; The elastic modulus (E) of the O-12 alloy is 95 GPa, while the shear modulus (G) is calculated to be 38 GPa.. Mechanism: Massive interstitial O atoms create strong, asymmetrical lattice distortions that impede dislocation nucleation and motion, while C and N segregation to grain boundaries reduces interfacial energy, stabilizing the boundaries against coarsening and suppressing localized shear deformation; this combination promotes dislocation multiplication and grain refinement without softening.. Limitations: The study notes that thermodynamic calculations cannot fully consider lattice distortions and interstitial site variations in concentrated solid solutions, and that Ga+ ion beam milling could potentially alter surface layers, though this was minimized.. Future work: The authors propose that the MISS alloy design strategy is applicable to a wide range of materials including alloys with multiple principal elements and may provide fundamental insights into plastic deformation in massive interstitially doped solid solutions.. Quote: "Here we introduce a class of massive interstitial solid solution (MISS) alloys by using a highly distorted substitutional host lattice, which enables solution of massive amounts of interstitials as an additional principal element class, without forming ceramic phases."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a single-phase high-entropy intermetallic alloy be designed to overcome the inherent brittleness of traditional intermetallics and achieve both high strength and extensive plasticity at room temperature and high homologous temperatures?. System: (CoNi)50(TiZrHf)50 (at. %) single-phase B2 high-entropy intermetallic alloy. Processing: Arc-melting high-purity raw materials (>99.9 wt.%) under Ti-gettered argon atmosphere, remelted at least five times, drop-cast into a copper mold, homogenized at 1000 °C for 24 h, and water quenched. Test conditions: Uniaxial compression from room temperature to ~0.9Tm (1582 K) at 1 × 10−3 s−1; microcompression on 1 μm diameter pillars at RT, 573 K, and 673 K; in situ STEM at RT and 573 K. Findings: Yield strength of ~1.5 GPa with plastic strain of ~8% at room temperature, which is about eight times that of conventional B2 alloys like NiAl and CoTi.; The alloy exhibits no precipitous thermal softening between homologous temperatures of 0.5 and 0.7, maintaining strength and strain hardening up to ~0.7Tm.; Micropillars with [100], [110], and [111] orientations show similar yield strength and elastic stiffness, indicating isotropic-like mechanical behavior.; Two slip systems, {110}<111> and {010}<100>, were identified with critical resolved shear stresses of 1235 ± 39 MPa and 1176 ± 245 MPa, respectively, differing by only 5%.; At room temperature, deformation induces local amorphization within slip bands, whereas at temperatures above 573 K, deformation results in dense dislocation forests without amorphization.; The velocity ratio of screw-to-edge dislocations was calculated to be ~0.6 at 300 K, significantly higher than the ~0.2 ratio in brittle BCC metals like tungsten.. Mechanism: Severe lattice distortion caused by atomic size and electronic property misfit mitigates atomic bonding differences along various crystal orientations, enabling dislocation multiplicity and isotropic behavior. Dislocation gliding disturbs the local chemical order, causing structural instability that leads to amorphization at low temperatures and the formation of local crystal-like order (dynamic hardening) at high temperatures, which impedes subsequent dislocation gliding and stabilizes plastic flow.. Limitations: The text notes that fracture at low temperatures may occur within amorphized regions and that the plastic strain at room temperature can vary (up to 27%) depending on machine stiffness, though this variability disappears at higher temperatures.. Future work: The authors suggest that manipulating the lattice distortion by adjusting the ratio of Co to Ni is a topic that warrants further research but is out of the scope of the current work.. Quote: "Unlike conventional intermetallics, this high-entropy alloy features a highly distorted crystalline lattice with complex chemical order, leading to multiple slip systems and high flow stress."

card: Paper card. Question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) affect the mobility mechanisms of screw and edge dislocations in the MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) across a wide temperature range?. System: MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA), specifically comparing random solid solution (RSS) and equilibrium SRO states at 800 K. Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using a moment tensor potential (MTP) machine-learning interatomic potential; SRO states equilibrated via hybrid MD/Monte Carlo (MD/MC) approach at 800 K. Test conditions: Temperatures from 300 K to 2000 K; applied shear stresses ranging from 0 to 3.0 GPa for screws and 0 to 1.0 GPa for edges; dislocation line length ~15 nm. Findings: At 300 K, SRO provides an extra strengthening of ~180 MPa for screw dislocations due to the formation of diffuse antiphase boundaries (DAPBs).; The strengthening effect of SRO on screw dislocations attenuates with increasing temperature, becoming negligible at 2000 K where mobility curves for RSS and SRO samples overlap.; A cross-slip locking mechanism involving the formation of jogs is observed for screw dislocations, providing extra strengthening independent of SRO presence.; Unlike screw dislocations, the mobility of edge dislocations is enhanced by the presence of SRO, particularly in the high-stress regime.; The SRO-induced enhancement of edge dislocation mobility extends to a characteristic length scale of approximately 1.2 nm into neighboring planes.; At 300 K, dislocation velocities in the MoNbTaW RHEA are significantly lower than in pure Mo and Nb, but this difference diminishes at 2000 K.; The attenuation of SRO strengthening at high temperatures is attributed to the increasing contribution of the entropy term (ΔS_kp) to the kink-pair formation free energy.. Mechanism: For screw dislocations, SRO creates an energy barrier (DAPB formation energy) that must be overcome during kink-pair nucleation, causing strengthening that is thermally activated and thus diminishes at high temperatures. For edge dislocations, SRO flattens the energy landscape, reducing solute drag effects and enhancing mobility despite the energy cost of disrupting order on the slip plane. Cross-slip locking in screws involves the formation of jogs on different slip planes that pin the dislocation line.. Limitations: The simulations use short dislocation line lengths (~15 nm) compared to realistic experimental conditions, meaning calculated velocities are dependent on this size and cannot be directly compared to macroscopic theoretical models without extrapolation. The study assumes the SRO state remains fixed during dislocation motion and does not account for changes in ordering around the moving core.. Future work: The authors state that predicting how the identified mechanisms combine to determine material strength requires appealing to mesoscale models for longer dislocation lengths and longer timescales, which is beyond the scope of the current work.. Quote: "The mobility of edge dislocations is found to be enhanced by the presence of SRO, whereas the rate of double-kink nucleation in the motion of screw dislocations is reduced."

Paper card. Question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) and temperature affect the mobility and friction stress of edge versus screw dislocations in a bcc MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) compared to pure bcc metals and binary alloys?. System: MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA), pure Mo, and binary Mo-Nb alloys (Mo95Nb5 to Mo75Nb25). Processing: Machine-learning interatomic potential (MTP) with radius cutoff (Rcut) of 4.7 Å and maximum level (levmax) of 14; MC/MD equilibration at 800 K; dislocation mobility simulations using LAMMPS with shear stress ramped at 20 MPa per 1.5 ps and held for 150 ps at temperatures of 300 K and 2000 K. Test conditions: Temperatures: 300 K and 2000 K; Shear stress ramp rate: 20 MPa per 1.5 ps; Hold time: 150 ps; Critical friction stress defined at 0.2 Å/ps for screw and 1.0 Å/ps for edge dislocations. Findings: The edge-to-screw velocity ratio decreases from 20 at 300 K to 11 at 2000 K in MoNbTaW.; Critical friction stress for edge dislocations decreases by 140 MPa from 300 to 2000 K.; Critical friction stress for screw dislocations decreases by 1.3 GPa (an order of magnitude larger) from 300 to 2000 K.; At ~2000 K, the critical friction stresses for both edge and screw dislocations decay to approximately the same level.; SRO hinders screw dislocation motion but accelerates edge dislocation motion in the RHEA.; A novel cross-slip locking mechanism was observed in the RHEA, attributed to intrinsic energy fluctuations and rugged energy landscapes.; Critical stress for screw dislocations follows an exponential decay with temperature, while edge dislocations follow a linear decrease.; Binary Mo-Nb alloys show lower critical friction stresses compared to the RHEA, with edge friction converging to zero in pure bcc metals.. Mechanism: Screw dislocations move via kink-pair nucleation and migration; SRO increases the free-energy barrier for kink-pair nucleation, causing temperature-dependent strengthening. Edge dislocations are accelerated by SRO through the attenuation of solute interaction magnitudes. The cross-slip locking mechanism arises from intrinsic energy fluctuations along the dislocation line and the rugged energy landscape.. Limitations: The study notes that the cross-slip locking mechanism was observed even with a limited cell size, implying potential size effects, and the phenomenological model is constructed specifically for the double-kink mechanism.. Future work: The authors state that the findings demonstrate mechanisms that can have a significant impact on mechanical properties, implying future work should explore these impacts, though no specific future experiments are explicitly detailed in the provided text.. Quote: "The edge-to-screw mobility ratio is around 20 at 300 K, which decreases to 11 when the temperature is raised to 2000 K."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the local destruction of short-range order (SRO) by dislocation glide lead to a rejuvenated state and influence the reversibility of planar defects (stacking faults and twin boundaries) in CrCoNi medium entropy alloys?. System: Equiatomic CrCoNi medium entropy alloy (MEA) and pure Ni single crystal. Processing: Water-quenched from 1200 °C for 48 h; twin-jet electrochemical polishing; FIB lift-out to MEMS chips; FIB patterning to create sharp crack; in situ push-to-pull cyclic loading in TEM at room temperature (300 K). Test conditions: Cyclic uniaxial tensile loading at room temperature (300 K); 1000 cycles; strain rate of 1 × 10^8 s^-1 in MD simulations; 300 keV electron beam for 4D-STEM; 15 eV and 20 eV energy filter slits. Findings: Average stacking fault (SF) length increased from 17.5 nm to 48.3 nm in the first cycle (t=T/2) but retracted to 22 nm upon unloading (t=T), indicating reversibility.; After 1000 cycles, SFs became irreversible with average length reaching 67.1 nm and twin boundaries reaching 124.2 nm at zero external load.; SF energy in pure Ni is approximately 120 mJ/m², while in CrCoNi MEA it is approximately 13.3 mJ/m² initially.; MD simulations show SF reversibility changes occur after around 20 cycles when SF energy drops below a threshold value.; Ni-Cr and Co-Co atomic pairs are insensitive to mechanical loading, while other SRO types show a steady decrease with cycle number.; Residual hydrostatic tensile strain ahead of the crack tip increased in Ni but decreased in CrCoNi MEA due to SF-mediated plasticity.; CrCoNi MEA showed more significant crack-tip blunting after 1000 cycles compared to Ni, suggesting rejuvenation promotes ductility.. Mechanism: Dislocation glide destroys local short-range order (SRO) on specific glide planes, leading to a rejuvenated state with higher entropy and free energy. This reduction in SRO lowers the stacking fault (SF) energy, making SFs and twin boundaries energetically favorable and irreversible, creating 'soft' zones that enhance damage tolerance.. Limitations: The study primarily focuses on quasi 2-dimensional models due to the constraints of in-situ TEM thin samples; the role of excess vacancies in defect evolution is considered minimal and possibly negligible.. Future work: Further studies on pure metals with low SF energy (like Cu) for comparison; identifying strategies to optimize the degree and distribution of SRO in MEAs/HEAs to coordinate local rejuvenation processes.. Quote: "Surprisingly, stacking faults (SFs) and twin boundaries (TBs) are reversible in initial cycles but become irreversible after a thousand cycles, indicating SF energy reduction and rejuvenation."

card: Paper card. Question: How do the strength, ductility, and fracture toughness of an equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy compare to high-entropy alloys and conventional materials, particularly at cryogenic temperatures, and what mechanisms drive these properties?. System: Equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA). Processing: Arc-melted high-purity elements (>99.9%) under argon, drop-cast into copper moulds, homogenized at 1,200 °C for 24 h, cold-forged and cross-rolled to ~10 mm thickness (60% reduction), then annealed at 800 °C for 1 h in air to achieve a recrystallized microstructure with 5–50 μm grains.. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at 293 K, 198 K, and 77 K with a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹; Compact-tension (C(T)) fracture toughness tests at 293 K, 198 K, and 77 K with fatigue pre-cracking and side-grooving per ASTM E1820.. Findings: At 77 K, yield strength reached 657 MPa and ultimate tensile strength reached 1,311 MPa, representing a ~50% increase from room temperature.; Tensile ductility (failure strain) increased to ~0.9 (90%) at 77 K, a ~25% increase from room temperature.; Fracture toughness (KJIc) at crack initiation increased from 208 MPa m1/2 at 293 K to 273 MPa m1/2 at 77 K.; Crack-growth toughness at 77 K reached critical stress-intensity values of ~430 MPa m1/2 (J ~900 kJ m⁻²).; The alloy exhibited a high strain-hardening exponent (n) of 0.4 at cryogenic temperatures.; The CrCoNi alloy showed ~15% higher tensile strength, ~30% higher ductility, and ~50% higher work of fracture than the five-component CrMnFeCoNi alloy at room temperature.; At 77 K, the CrCoNi alloy displayed ~25% higher KJIc, ~27% higher ductility, and ~31% higher work of fracture compared to the CrMnFeCoNi alloy.. Mechanism: The exceptional damage tolerance results from continuous steady strain hardening that suppresses plastic instability, driven by pronounced dislocation activity and deformation-induced nano-twinning. Nano-twinning acts as a dominant deformation mode that provides a steady source of strain hardening, delaying necking and accommodating strain, with its intensity increasing as temperature decreases from room temperature to 77 K.. Limitations: The yield strength at 77 K was slightly lower than the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, attributed to the non-uniform grain size of the current material; the volume fraction of void-initiating inclusions was not accurately quantified relative to the five-component alloy.. Future work: Further studies are needed to accurately determine the relative volume fractions of void-initiating inclusions in the MEA and HEA and to identify their chemistry and crystal structure by TEM after extraction from the voids.. Quote: "strength, ductility and toughness of the CrCoNi alloy improve to strength levels above 1.3 GPa, failure strains up to 90% and KJIc values of 275 MPa m1/2."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the capacity for twinning-controlled deformation in the equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy generate a simultaneous increase in strength and ductility, and what is the origin of its exceptional fracture toughness?. System: Nominally equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with a single-phase face-centered cubic (fcc) structure. Processing: Samples extracted from a previously produced alloy; micro-pillars (~300 nm diameter) machined using focused-ion beam (FIB) techniques; in situ TEM compression tests performed at 300 kV; in situ TEM tensile tests conducted at room temperature using a Gatan model 654 single-tilt straining holder at 200 kV; DFT calculations performed using VASP with the nudged-elastic band method. Test conditions: Room temperature (300 K); uniaxial tension and compression; micro-pillar compression at 300 kV; in situ straining at 10 frames per second; DFT calculations at 0 K and 500 K. Findings: The alloy exhibits high strength (~1 GPa), ductility (~60% uniform elongation), and exceptional fracture toughness (KIc > 200 MPa√m).; Ab initio calculations reveal a negative intrinsic stacking-fault energy (γisf = −23 mJ m−2) at 0 K and a high twinnability value (τta = 1.07 ± 0.02).; Deformation activates three twinning systems within individual coarse grains (5–50 μm), forming a stable 3D hierarchical twin network with twin thicknesses ranging from ~100 nm to several micrometres.; Micro-pillars containing a pre-existing {111} twin boundary showed a maximum strength exceeding 2.5 GPa, approximately 1 GPa higher than pillars without a twin.; Dislocations pile up at coherent twin boundaries (CTBs), acting as strong barriers to motion, while intersecting twin boundaries serve as fast channels for dislocation glide.; Dislocations cross-slip between intersecting twin boundaries via an 'overpass' mechanism, enabling homogeneous plastic deformation in three dimensions.; The 3D twin architecture remains stable during deformation with no evidence of twin growth or de-twinning, even as dislocations move rapidly along the boundaries.. Mechanism: The 3D hierarchical twin network provides a dual function: conventional strengthening occurs via the blockage of dislocations impinging on twin boundaries, while the interconnected network offers pathways for dislocation glide along and cross-slip between intersecting twin-matrix interfaces, allowing simultaneous high strength and ductility.. Limitations: The study notes that nano-pillar tests investigate limited volumes; detailed processes of sessile dislocation involvement in cross-slip were not fully captured due to limited time-resolution of in situ TEM; the specific role of magnetization was analyzed but calculations were mainly performed on non-magnetic structures.. Future work: The authors propose that documenting this enhanced twinning-induced toughness may present new directions for the future design of metallic alloys with unprecedented combinations of mechanical properties.. Quote: "This serves a dual function: conventional twin-boundary (TB) strengthening from blockage of dislocations impinging on TBs, coupled with the 3D twin network which offers pathways for dislocation glide along, and cross-slip between, intersecting TB-matrix interfaces."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the deformation and failure mechanisms of an equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy subjected to extreme shock loading (strain rates >10^6/s), and how do pre-existing defects influence void nucleation, growth, and coalescence?. System: Equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA), single-phase face-centered cubic (fcc), cold rolled 80% and annealed at 1000°C for 48 hours (grain size ~100 μm). Processing: Pulsed laser-driven shock experiments at the Omega laser facility (352-nm wavelength, 1 ns pulse, 100–150 J for VISAR, up to 450 J per beam for spallation); recovery of samples for multiscale characterization (STEM, EBSD, TEM, FIB); Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations using LAMMPS with an embedded atom model potential (single-crystal ~3.84 million atoms, piston-driven shock compression at 5 K, tensile loading at 10^7 s^-1 and 500 K). Test conditions: Strain rates estimated at ~1 × 10^7/s; shock pressures up to 130 GPa (ablation pressure); tensile spall loading upon shock wave release; temperatures estimated to rise locally by a factor of two near voids; strain rates in MD simulations of 10^7 s^-1. Findings: Spall strength was estimated to be approximately 9.8 GPa at a strain rate of ~1 × 10^7/s.; Shock compression generated a three-dimensional network of planar defects including stacking faults, nanotwins, and hexagonal nanolamella on {111} planes.; Nanoindentation showed a 30% increase in hardness in moderately laser-shocked samples compared to as-received material.; Voids nucleated preferentially in amorphous regions formed at intersections of planar defects and at grain boundaries.; Voids near grain boundaries were generally larger (>20 μm) and more susceptible to coalescence than those in grain interiors.; MD simulations showed that pre-existing nanotwins constrained dislocation glide, changing void geometry from uniform to penny-shaped.; The presence of nanotwins delayed void coalescence, keeping two voids separated under the same applied volumetric strain compared to defect-free samples.; Amorphization occurred in heavily deformed regions where local defect density was sufficiently high, confirmed by reduced radial distribution function peak intensity.. Mechanism: During shock compression, the low stacking fault energy (SFE) of CrCoNi promotes the homogeneous nucleation of planar defects (stacking faults, twins, hcp lamella) forming a 3D nanointerface network. Upon shock release, tensile stress triggers void nucleation, which occurs preferentially in amorphous regions created by defect intersections and at grain boundaries. During void growth, the pre-existing planar defects constrain the emission and glide of dislocation loops from the void surface, altering void geometry (anisotropic growth) and delaying coalescence, thereby enhancing spall strength and damage tolerance. Thermal softening and shear localization can also occur, leading to nanorecrystallization and amorphization.. Limitations: The nominal strain rate is not constant due to rapid stress wave decay; systematic experiments at various temperatures and strain rates are needed to quantitatively explore the Zener-Hollomon relationship; the specific effect of amorphization on mechanical behavior is still debated; the results may not be unique to HEAs but also apply to fcc metals with low SFE.. Future work: Conduct systematic experiments at various temperatures and strain rates to quantitatively explore the Zener-Hollomon relationship; tailor the SFE of these materials to promote TWIP, TRIP, and amorphization effects to further improve impact resistance; investigate the specific effect of amorphization on mechanical behavior.. Quote: "Molecular dynamics simulations corroborate the experimental results and suggest that deformation-induced defects formed before void nucleation govern the geometry of void growth and delay their coalescence."

card: Paper card. Question: How can machine learning and molecular dynamics be combined to predict the optimal composition, mechanical properties, and tension-compression asymmetry of FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloys, and what is the mechanism by which HEA coatings affect the mechanical properties of a nickel matrix?. System: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloys (specifically Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13) and Ni matrix with HEA coating. Processing: Molecular dynamics simulations using LAMMPS with EAM potential; model size 3.56 × 7.12 × 3.56 nm³; relaxed at 300 K under NVT ensemble for 300 ps; strain rate 4 × 10⁻⁷ s⁻¹; time step 0.001 ps; Machine Learning using Multiple Linear Regression (MLR), Back Propagation Neural Network (BPNN), and Random Forest (RF) with 80% training/20% test split. Test conditions: Tensile and compressive loads applied in y direction at temperatures of 77 K, 300 K, 600 K, and 900 K; atomic content limits 5% to 35% for ML input. Findings: The MLR model predicted an optimal composition of Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 with a tensile strength of 28.25 GPa.; The error between the MLR predicted tensile strength (28.25 GPa) and the MD simulated tensile strength (28.38 GPa) was within 0.5%.; Tensile strength of FeNiCrCoCu HEA increased significantly with Ni content, while Co and Cu content showed a trend of increasing then decreasing strength.; Tension-compression asymmetry increased with temperature (40.5% at 77 K to 73.94% at 600 K) and Cu content, but decreased with Fe content.; Polycrystalline HEA tensile and compressive strengths decreased by 31.33% and 30.03% respectively at 300 K compared to single crystal HEA.; HEA coating increased Ni tensile strength from 2.3 GPa to 2.46 GPa and reduced Ni tension-compression asymmetry from 65.97% to 48.8%.; The MLR model achieved a prediction confidence of 84.9%, higher than BPNN (68.28%) and RF (74.94%).. Mechanism: Tension-compression asymmetry is caused by twinning increasing stress during compression and dislocation slip reducing stress during tension; HEA coating reduces asymmetry in Ni by promoting dislocation climb and twin formation in the matrix, where different atomic sizes obstruct slip and stress concentration promotes twinning, while twin degradation at the interface reduces compressive strength.. Limitations: The study relies on molecular dynamics simulations which may not capture all experimental complexities; the text notes that experimental methods require significant cost and time, implying the simulation is a substitute but does not explicitly state simulation limitations beyond the scope of the provided text.. Quote: "The optimal multiple linear regression machine learning algorithm predicts that the optimal composition is Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 high-entropy alloy, with a tensile strength of 28.25 GPa."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the number of metallic elements in multi-component high-entropy alloys affect their resistance to interdiffusion between Cu and Si, and what are the structural and thermodynamic mechanisms responsible for this suppression?. System: Six alloy systems: unitary Ti (1A), binary TiTa (2A), ternary TiTaCr (3A), quaternary TiTaCrZr (4A), quinary TiTaCrZrAl (5A), and senary TiTaCrZrAlRu (6A); used as ~7 nm diffusion barrier layers (DBnA) in Si/DBnA/Cu stacks.. Processing: Magnetron sputtering at room temperature; RF power 150 W, substrate bias -100 V, Ar atmosphere (30 sccm, 6 × 10⁻³ torr); Cu top layer (50 nm) deposited at 50 W; thermal annealing in N₂/H₂ (5% H₂) at 300–900°C for 30 min (5°C/min ramp).. Test conditions: Thermal annealing from 300°C to 900°C; failure defined by Cu penetration into Si forming Cu silicides; characterized via SEM, XRD, electrical resistivity, TEM, and EDS line scanning.. Findings: Failure temperature of Si/DBnA/Cu stacks increased from 550°C (unitary Ti) to 900°C (senary TiTaCrZrAlRu) with more elements.; Activation energy of Cu diffusion increased from 110 kJ/mol (unitary) to 163 kJ/mol (senary), a difference of 53 kJ/mol.; Lattice distortion strain energy increased to 16.8 kJ/mol for quaternary alloys and remained high (11.9–14.6 kJ/mol) for quinary/senary alloys.; Average cohesive energy increased by up to 38.1 kJ/mol in the senary alloy compared to the unitary alloy (14.2 kJ/mol).; Packing density increased from 0.680 (bcc-based binary) to 0.711 (senary), reducing free volume and vacancy concentration.; Theoretical total increase in activation energy (55 kJ/mol) closely matched the experimental increase (53 kJ/mol).; Amorphous senary alloy remained stable up to 800°C, whereas unitary Ti crystallized at 500°C.. Mechanism: Suppressed interdiffusion is caused by three dominant factors: (1) structural lattice distortion strain energy elongates diffusion paths and increases vacancy formation difficulty; (2) increased cohesive energy raises the bond-breaking energy required for atom movement; and (3) higher packing density reduces free volume, diminishing vacancy concentration. Together, these thermodynamic and structural factors increase the activation energy for substitutional Cu diffusion via vacancies.. Limitations: Small differences between experimental and theoretical activation energies may be attributable to a 'volume-to-area' effect, as diffusion models are typically 2D while calculations are 3D; also, exact composition of thin barriers may slightly vary from thick films due to thickness dependence.. Future work: Further investigation is needed to clarify the possibility of short-range ordering existing within the amorphous matrix of the alloy barriers.. Quote: "with more elements incorporated, the failure temperature of the barriers increased from 550 to 900°C."
